prompt: Which description of a hallucination matches how it comes about?
hint: Lesson 1: what does a model write, every time?

choices.text: The likeliest continuation, at a moment when it is false
choices.why: Right. The same step produces the right answers and the invented ones.

choices.text: A rare fault in the model's hardware
choices.why: Nothing breaks. The model is doing exactly what it always does.

choices.text: The model lying on purpose to please you
choices.why: It has no purpose to lie with. It writes what is likely.

choices.text: A lookup that fetched the wrong row from a database of facts
choices.why: There is no database of facts inside the model, and no lookup.

prompt: `toylm generate "the soup of the day is" --samples 5` answered tomato three times, pumpkin once and lentil once. Which statement is true?
hint: What does the file say about today?

choices.text: Tomato is today's soup, since it won three of the five draws
choices.why: It won because the file mentions it most. That says nothing about today.

choices.text: The model is broken, since it disagrees with itself
choices.why: Drawing in proportion to the scores is expected to give different answers (lesson 1).

choices.text: Lentil is false, since it came up only once
choices.why: Lentil is as likely to be today's soup as tomato. Nothing in the file says either way.

choices.text: Each answer is likely, and none is known
choices.why: Yes. The file lists soups from several days and says nothing about today.

prompt: What score did `toylm next "the owner of the café is"` give to `full`?
hint: Read the percentage on the only line.

prompt: How many times does the word `owner` occur in the corpus, according to `grep -c`?
Why did `toylm` give `full` 100% after `the owner of the café is`?

choices.text: The corpus says the owner is full
choices.why: The corpus never mentions an owner; `grep -c` found none.

choices.text: Its window held `café is`, and in the corpus `café is` is followed by `full` every time
choices.why: Right. The score measures the file's consistency after those two words, not anything about owners.

choices.text: A score of 100% means it checked the answer first
choices.why: Nothing was checked. A score is a share of counts.

choices.text: The temperature was 0
choices.why: `toylm next` prints the scores before any temperature is applied.

prompt: A model gives an answer a very high probability. What does that tell you?

choices.text: How consistent its training text was after that context
choices.why: Right. The high score sat on `full`, an answer with nothing to do with the question.

choices.text: How likely the answer is to be true
choices.why: Likely and true are different things. `full` was 100% and is not an answer about owners.

choices.text: How many sources confirmed the answer before it was written
choices.why: No sources are consulted. The score comes from the model's weights or, here, counts.

choices.text: How carefully the model reasoned
choices.why: No reasoning is involved in a score; it is the output of one step.

prompt: Why does an invented citation look exactly like a real one?
hint: Look at the last row of the table.

choices.text: The model copies a real paper and changes the names
choices.why: It does not copy and edit. It writes each piece as the likely continuation.

choices.text: The model checks that the journal exists but not the article
choices.why: It checks nothing. Every part of the citation is generated the same way.

choices.text: Invented citations contain a hidden marker that only software can detect
choices.why: There is no marker. Looking the reference up is the way to find out.

choices.text: Citations follow a pattern
choices.why: Right, and the model continues the pattern as fluently as a sentence. The form is all you can see.

prompt: Which of these requests are especially prone to a confident wrong answer? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: A fact that is rare in the text the model learnt from
choices.why: Yes: a common pattern about something similar tends to win.

choices.text: A fact that has changed since the training text was written
choices.why: Yes: the old value was in far more of the text, and it comes back in the present tense.

choices.text: A question built on a false premise
choices.why: Yes: text that answers a question is likelier than text that disputes it.

choices.text: Repeating a sentence that is in the prompt you sent
choices.why: The sentence is in front of the model, so copying it is the likely continuation. That is why grounding works.

prompt: Why has training not removed hallucination?
hint: What would the model need in order to check itself?

choices.text: Nobody has tried to train models to admit uncertainty
choices.why: They have, and models have improved. The problem shrinks without going away.

choices.text: Hallucination happens only with older models
choices.why: Newer models hallucinate less, and they still do.

choices.text: The model has no separate store of facts to check its text against
choices.why: Right. What it knows and what it finds likely are the same thing inside it.

choices.text: It is caused by a bug that is fixed in every new version
choices.why: It is not a bug. It comes from the same step that produces correct answers.

prompt: Why does adding "Do not make things up" to a prompt help so little?
hint: Could the model follow it if it wanted to?

choices.text: Models ignore every instruction that is phrased as a negative
choices.why: Negative instructions are followed often enough. This one asks for something the model cannot see.

choices.text: The model does not know which of its likely answers are invented
choices.why: Right. If it could tell, it would not write them.

choices.text: The sentence is too short to have any effect
choices.why: Length is not the problem. The model has nothing to check its answers against.

choices.text: The instruction is removed by the provider before the request reaches the model
choices.why: Nothing removes it. It reaches the model and cannot be acted on.

prompt: `retrieve --prompt` numbers each source. What does the number add?
hint: What can a reader do with `[1]`?

choices.text: The reply names the source it used, which makes it checkable
choices.why: Yes. A reader or a program goes to source 1 and sees whether it says that.

choices.text: It ranks the sources by how true they are
choices.why: The order comes from keyword matching, which says nothing about truth.

choices.text: Numbers make a model obey instructions
choices.why: They are labels for citing. They change nothing about obedience.

choices.text: It stops the model from using general knowledge
choices.why: The instruction asks for that. The numbers make the reply checkable.

prompt: For "Who owns the café?", retrieval returned two lines about opening hours. Why does the instruction's second sentence matter here?
hint: What is the likeliest continuation of a question?

choices.text: It makes retrieval find a passage about the owner
choices.why: Retrieval had already run. The handbook has no such passage.

choices.text: It forbids the model from mentioning the café
choices.why: It does no such thing. It says what to reply when the sources lack the answer.

choices.text: It tells the model to search the internet when the handbook has no answer
choices.why: It says the opposite: do not answer from general knowledge.

choices.text: It gives the model an honest way out
choices.why: Right: saying the handbook does not say becomes a likely reply instead of an invented owner.

prompt: `grep -rF` found the first quote in `refunds.md` and found the second nowhere. What does that show about a reply built on the second quote?
hint: What can a program check without judging anything?

choices.text: The handbook is incomplete and should be updated
choices.why: The handbook is fine. The quote was invented.

choices.text: `grep` failed, because quotes need a smarter search
choices.why: An exact quote is exactly what `grep -F` finds.

choices.text: The reply is wrong only if a person agrees
choices.why: No judgement is needed: the sentence is either in the file or it is not.

choices.text: The claim it rests on has no source
choices.why: Right. A quote missing from the source is a hallucination caught automatically.

prompt: At temperature 0, `toylm` said tomato three times out of three. What should you conclude?

choices.text: Tomato is now confirmed as today's soup
choices.why: Three runs of the same rule agree with each other by construction. Nothing was confirmed.

choices.text: Temperature 0 is the setting that prevents hallucination
choices.why: It removes variety, not error. The answer is the same and still unknown.

choices.text: It is consistent, which is not the same as correct
choices.why: Right. It repeats the likeliest answer, including when the likeliest answer is invented.

choices.text: The model has learnt from the earlier draws
choices.why: Nothing changes in the model between runs.

prompt: If the sources do not contain the answer, the instruction from `retrieve --prompt` asks for the reply "the handbook does not ___".
hint: The verb in the instruction's second sentence.

prompt: A reply cites a web page that supports its claim. What is the cheapest useful check?
hint: Each reference either exists or does not.

choices.text: Open the link
choices.why: Right. It takes a minute, and an invented reference fails at once.

choices.text: Ask the same model whether the link is real
choices.why: Its answer about the link comes from the same likely-text step as the link itself.

choices.text: Trust it if the address looks like a real site's
choices.why: An invented link has the right shape; that is why it is convincing.

choices.text: Run the prompt again at a lower temperature
choices.why: That makes the same reply more consistent, not more correct.

prompt: Put a grounded answer, checked, in order.
hint: It starts before the model is asked anything.
items: Find the passages that match the question
Put them in the prompt, numbered, with the instruction
The model replies and quotes the source it used
Check each quote against the source

prompt: Match each remedy to what it does.
hint: The headings of the second section.

pairs.right: puts the true text where the model can see it
makes an honest refusal a likely reply
makes a claim checkable by a program

right_distractors: makes every answer the model gives true
